title: Trump’s Middle East Dealmaking Is Working Against Itself
gist: Eitan Danon and Joshua Kram argue the Trump administration's Middle East deal spree (UAE AI chips, Saudi F-35s and civil nuclear deal, Syria sanctions relief, possible Turkey F-35s) arms all sides of deepening rivalries among U.S. partners and risks an arms race and duplicative national AI stacks. They propose interagency review of bilateral deals, conditioning arms, nuclear and chip access on cooperation, and a regional coordinator to ensure strategic coherence.

insights.claim: In a few months the Trump administration signed a Jordan trade deal, granted the UAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips, lifted Syria sanctions, approved F-35 sales to Saudi Arabia, approved a major Israel arms package and signed a Saudi civil nuclear agreement.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: A pipeline of contracts for U.S. defense, nuclear and AI-chip companies in the Gulf.
insights.locator: The Trump administration has been on

insights.claim: The authors argue that because U.S. partners are increasingly one another's rivals, Washington is arming and equipping all sides of the region's rifts without a theory of how to weigh deals against one another.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Commercial wins today may translate into higher regional conflict risk later.
insights.quote: Washington is arming and equipping all sides of the region’s many rifts

insights.claim: The Saudi civil nuclear deal approved in August and the F-35 sale approved in September are both still pending congressional approval.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Congressional action is a near-term catalyst for defense and nuclear contractors.

insights.claim: Turkey remains banned by U.S. law from buying the F-35 until it gives up its Russian S-400 system, though Trump said he would consider allowing it.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Any Turkey F-35 move hinges on resolving the S-400 issue.

insights.claim: The Iran war has deepened rifts among U.S. partners: Saudi-Israel normalization is frozen, Saudi Arabia joined Pakistan and Turkey in the Mecca defense pact, and Israel and the UAE are cooperating more closely.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Realigning blocs raise the risk of intra-partner conflict in a key energy region.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and the UAE, once aligned, are now openly competing for regional leadership in economics and technology.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Gulf rivalry drives competing mega-investments and could split OPEC+ cohesion or capital flows.

insights.claim: Israel and Turkey have grown increasingly antagonistic, including over Syria, and Israel and Greece signed a historic defense deal this summer to check Turkish influence.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Eastern Mediterranean security alignments are hardening.

themes.theme: Arms race and erosion of Israel's qualitative edge

insights.claim: Because Israel, Turkey, the UAE and Saudi Arabia all have advanced fighters and nuclear know-how yet remain acute competitors, the authors warn U.S. deals could fuel a regional arms race and erode Israel's qualitative military edge.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Supports sustained Gulf defense procurement demand but raises proliferation risk.
insights.quote: these deals could fuel a regional arms race and erode Israel’s qualitative military edge

insights.claim: Unlike China and India, which pursue bilateral Middle East deals without being security guarantors, the United States has far more to lose if partners like Israel and Turkey or Saudi Arabia and the UAE clash.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: U.S. exposure to regional conflict is asymmetric relative to commercial rivals.
insights.quote: neither China nor India has been a security guarantor in the region

insights.claim: China signs tens of billions of dollars a year in Belt and Road construction contracts across the Middle East and signed a 25-year framework with Iran in 2021 while remaining the GCC's largest trading partner.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: China's balanced commercial footprint is a benchmark for U.S. strategy.

themes.theme: Competing Gulf AI stacks on U.S. tech

insights.claim: Stargate UAE, part of a planned 5-gigawatt Abu Dhabi campus built around G42 with OpenAI, Cisco, Nvidia, SoftBank and Oracle, anchors the UAE's ambition to be a global AI hub.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Large Gulf AI infrastructure demand for U.S. chip, networking and cloud vendors.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's PIF-backed HUMAIN is pursuing a parallel AI hub with Nvidia and Amazon Web Services, creating two national AI stacks on the same U.S. technology under separate bilateral terms.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Duplicative Gulf AI buildouts expand near-term demand for Nvidia and hyperscalers.

insights.claim: The authors argue U.S. AI deals in the Gulf are creating duplication rather than synergy on a critical emerging technology.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Possible future overcapacity risk in Gulf AI data centers.
insights.quote: U.S. deals are creating duplication rather than synergy on a critical emerging technology

insights.claim: U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack said America is no longer the world's guarantor and has no playbook, going 'one play at a time,' reflecting the view that bilateral deals are the strategy.
insights.speaker: Tom Barrack
insights.so_what: Signals a transactional U.S. posture with less security underwriting for partners.
insights.quote: “America as the guarantor to the world, for the last 80 years, it is no longer there. …We don’t have a playbook. We’re all on audibles. We can go one play at a time.”

insights.claim: The authors concede Barrack is partly right that the U.S. has historically overstated its ability to smooth regional rivalries, but argue Washington should not aggravate fault lines that will ultimately hurt it.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Expect continued uncoordinated deal flow absent policy change.

insights.claim: The authors propose a White House review process for major bilateral deals, akin to outbound investment screening, so the whole government can assess region-wide impacts before agreements are finalized.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Could add approval friction and timeline risk for Gulf defense and tech deals.

insights.claim: They suggest the U.S. Economic Diplomacy Action Group chaired by Marco Rubio and the Pax Silica AI supply-chain initiative, which includes the UAE, Qatar and Israel, as platforms to reconcile deals and promote shared standards.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Pax Silica may become a gatekeeper for Gulf access to U.S. AI supply chains.

insights.claim: They recommend tying Turkey arms sales to Syria deconfliction with Israel, Saudi civil nuclear cooperation to Syria reconstruction investment, and AI chip export licenses to common security standards.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Conditionality could slow chip export approvals while channeling Gulf capital into Syria.

insights.claim: They urge U.S. backing for cross-border projects without requiring Abraham Accords membership, such as Gulf-to-Turkey rail through the Levant, electricity infrastructure and regional desalination.
insights.speaker: Eitan Danon, Joshua Kram
insights.so_what: Flags potential infrastructure, power and water investment themes in the region.
